name: Black Manhattan
desc: A richer, more bitter Manhattan built with Averna amaro in place of sweet vermouth — or Barolo Chinato for the premium expression. Deeper, earthier, more complex. The Barolo Chinato version is the special-occasion build and what confirmed this as a personal favorite.
glass: Rocks glass over large single cube · or coupe up

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Bottled-in-bond, 100 proof — the spice cuts right through the amaro. The canonical choice and exceptional value. This is the one to own.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Vermont rye, 100 proof, aged 10 years. More rounded and honeyed than Rittenhouse. The amaro plays differently — slightly richer, less punchy.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Finished in Madeira, Sauternes, and Cognac casks. Adds wine and dried-fruit complexity that mirrors and amplifies the Barolo Chinato version specifically.

ingredients.name: Averna Amaro · or · Cocchi Barolo Chinato (premium)

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Caramel-forward, herbal, slightly sweet. The most approachable and versatile amaro you can own. Your everyday build.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Wine-based, bitter, complex — more like a sophisticated vermouth than a standard amaro. What you had the night this became a favorite. The premium build. Worth every penny of the ~$55 price.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Not an upgrade in price but a flavor shift: Ramazzotti is drier and more bitter than Averna; Cynar (artichoke-based) is darker and earthier. Both move the drink away from sweetness toward deep bitterness.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Dry, spicy, and complex — the bartender's standard. Bridges the rye and amaro beautifully. Don't skip this; it completes the drink in a way Angostura alone doesn't.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Slightly fruitier and softer than Regans'. A valid alternative; some prefer it in this specific build for its rounder orange note.

steps: Chill your glass — rocks glass in the freezer, or fill it with ice water while you build the drink.
Combine rye, Averna (or Barolo Chinato), Angostura, and orange bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25–30 seconds — full dilution and integration. The amaro needs time to marry with the rye.
Strain over a large single ice cube in a rocks glass, or into a chilled coupe up. Express orange twist over the surface if using, then drop it in alongside the Luxardo cherry.
notes: Two builds: The Averna version is your everyday drink — approachable, herbal, slightly sweet. The Barolo Chinato version is special occasion — more bitter, more complex, wine-forward. Know which you're making before you pour.
The orange bitters matter: Angostura alone doesn't bridge the herbal gap between amaro and rye. A single dash of Regans' does that job. Don't skip it.
Garnish: Luxardo cherries only. The neon-red grocery store maraschino is a completely different product. Orange twist is optional but adds aromatic lift, especially in the Barolo Chinato version.
Variation — Smoked Black Manhattan: Split the rye 50/50 with a peated blended Scotch (Compass Box Smokey). The Averna reads differently against smoke — more herbal, less sweet.
history: The Black Manhattan was created by Todd Smith at Bourbon & Branch in San Francisco around 2005, substituting Averna amaro for sweet vermouth. It spread rapidly through the craft cocktail world because it solved a real problem: sweet vermouth can overwhelm a well-made rye. The amaro brings bitterness and herbal complexity that amplifies the whiskey rather than competing with it. The Barolo Chinato variation uses a wine-based digestif from Piedmont — a grape-and-quinine aperitif that adds tannin and bitter wine depth that standard amaro doesn't provide.

name: Toronto
desc: Rye whiskey with Fernet-Branca as the modifier. Bold, medicinal, assertive — Fernet announces itself, but the high-proof rye holds its ground. One of the most aggressively spirit-forward cocktails in the Manhattan family.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Essential here — Fernet is aggressive and medicinal, and a low-proof whiskey simply disappears behind it.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Lighter and more floral than Rittenhouse, which lets Fernet's menthol and licorice come forward more.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: More rounded and oak-forward. The Fernet reads differently — less of a clash, more of a conversation.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: 27 herbs, menthol-forward, medicinal, intensely bitter. A quarter ounce is intentional — start here.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Shifts menthol from background to foreground. Changes the drink's character entirely — more polarizing but interesting.

steps: Combine rye, Fernet, simple syrup, and Angostura bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds until well-chilled.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express orange peel over the glass and drop it in, or discard.
notes: On the Fernet: ¼ oz is precise. Fernet contains saffron, myrrh, chamomile, and 23 other botanicals plus significant menthol. Dial up only after you've made it once and know you want more.
Simple syrup: Just enough to round Fernet's edges. It's structural — the drink should not taste sweet.
Variation — Toronto Sour: Add ¾ oz fresh lemon juice and shake instead of stir. The Fernet reads completely differently against citrus — more medicinal herb than aggressive bitter.
history: The Toronto is a classic Prohibition-era cocktail, likely developed in Canada where rye was legal and Fernet was available as medicine. It fell out of fashion for decades and was revived by the craft cocktail movement — Death & Co in New York was instrumental in putting it back on menus.

name: Vieux Carré
desc: A New Orleans classic — rye and cognac as co-equal bases, bridged by Bénédictine, with both sweet vermouth and both bitters. Essentially two Manhattan variants sharing a glass. Rich, layered, and complex.
glass: Rocks glass · Single large ice cube

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Provides spice and backbone against the rounder cognac.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: The New Orleans native choice — more delicate and floral, which complements the cognac rather than competing with it.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The right price point for cocktail use.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Made specifically for cocktails — higher proof, more robust, designed to hold its own against assertive modifiers.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Lighter and more floral — changes the whole balance toward finesse.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Rich, chocolatey, and complex — far superior to generic sweet vermouth in this build.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: The classic choice for this drink — Carpano Antica was invented in Turin in 1786 and the Vieux Carré was built around this style of vermouth.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds until well-chilled.
Strain over a large single ice cube in a rocks glass.
Express a lemon or orange peel and drop it in.
notes: Bénédictine: One teaspoon only — it's made from 27 plants and spices. The herbal honey-spice quality should weave through the drink, not lead it.
Both bitters: Peychaud's is lighter and anise-forward; Angostura is spicier and deeper. Together they create complexity neither achieves alone.
Variation — The Maximilian Affair: Replace the cognac with mezcal. Structurally similar but smoke dramatically changes the character.
history: Created at the Hotel Monteleone in New Orleans around 1938 by head bartender Walter Bergeron. Named for the French Quarter, it was designed as a celebration of New Orleans' cosmopolitan influences — rye for American tradition, cognac for French heritage, Bénédictine for European monastery culture.

name: Penicillin
desc: Blended Scotch, honey-ginger syrup, lemon, with a peated Islay Scotch float. Smoke leads every sip — the lemon and honey are structural, not the headline. The drink that proved the sour format can work when smoke and bitterness are out front.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The canonical Penicillin base — light enough not to compete with the Laphroaig float, complex enough to provide backbone.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Richer and maltier. The honey-ginger reads slightly more dessert-adjacent.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Already heavily peated — combining with the Laphroaig float creates an intensely smoky drink. For when you want smoke fully in charge.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: 1 cup honey + 1 cup water + 2 oz fresh sliced ginger. Simmer 5 min, cool, strain. Keeps 2 weeks refrigerated.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The most aggressively peated mainstream Scotch — iodine, seaweed, phenolic smoke. The float means it hits your nose and palate first on every sip.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More campfire and charcoal, less medicinal iodine. Some find it more elegant; others prefer Laphroaig's aggression.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Same phenolic smoke, mellowed and deepened by 18 years of aging.

steps: Make honey-ginger syrup: combine 1 cup honey, 1 cup water, and 2 oz fresh sliced ginger in a saucepan. Warm until honey dissolves, simmer 5 minutes, cool completely, strain. Keeps 2 weeks refrigerated.
Combine blended Scotch, honey-ginger syrup, and fresh lemon juice in a shaker with ice.
Shake vigorously for 10–12 seconds.
Strain over a large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Float the Laphroaig: pour gently over the back of a bar spoon held just above the surface so it sits on top.
Garnish with a piece of candied ginger on a pick.
notes: The float is non-negotiable: Don't stir it in. The Laphroaig on top means the first thing hitting you is peat and smoke. Stirred, it becomes a pleasant but much less interesting smoky sour.
Fresh lemon only: Bottled lemon juice is a different product. The Penicillin is more sensitive to ingredient quality than most cocktails.
Variation — The Prescription: Replace the blended Scotch with bourbon. The Laphroaig float becomes contrast rather than continuation — a very different but compelling drink.
history: Created by Sam Ross at Milk & Honey in New York around 2005, the Penicillin is widely regarded as one of the most important cocktails of the modern craft era. The float technique was the key insight — by keeping the Islay Scotch separate, every sip delivers a different experience from nose to finish.

name: Oaxacan Old Fashioned
desc: Phil Ward's Death & Co classic. Structurally an Old Fashioned, but the tequila-mezcal split and mole bitters make it a completely different experience. The smoke anchors everything the way bourbon's vanilla usually does.
glass: Rocks glass · Single large ice cube

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Women-owned Jalisco distillery, clean and slightly oaky. Excellent cocktail tequila at a fair price.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Tahona-milled, more earthy and agave-forward.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: One of the most respected small-production reposados. Rich, complex, deeply agave-forward.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The benchmark lightly smoky mezcal — earthy, fruity, subtle smoke. The original and correct choice.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More mineral and savory than Vida. The smoke is drier.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.bottle: Del Maguey San Luis del Rio
tiers.note: Single-village, significantly more complex and smoky. Reserve for when you want mezcal to be the conversation.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Chocolate, cinnamon, dried chili — designed for this cocktail. Not substitutable.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: The Angostura's allspice and clove adds depth beneath the mole bitters' chocolate-chili character.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds.
Strain over a large single ice cube.
Express orange peel and drop it in.
notes: Agave nectar: Dilute 2:1 (agave:water) before using — straight agave is too viscous. One teaspoon is precise.
Mole bitters: Not optional. Without them this is just a mezcal old fashioned.
Variation — Full Mezcal: Drop the tequila and use 2 oz mezcal. Dramatically smokier — a different drink.
history: Created by Phil Ward at Death & Co in New York around 2007, the Oaxacan Old Fashioned single-handedly validated mezcal as a serious cocktail spirit in the American market. Ward's insight was treating it as a modifier rather than a base, letting tequila carry the structure while mezcal provided smoke and complexity.

name: Naked and Famous
desc: Equal parts mezcal, Aperol, yellow Chartreuse, fresh lime. The mezcal anchors the smoke the way bourbon's vanilla does in the Paper Plane original — keeping sweetness from taking over.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Enough smoke to anchor the Aperol, not so much it overwhelms the Chartreuse.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Smokier than Vida — shifts the center of gravity toward the mezcal. Pushes closer to your wheelhouse.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The orange-bitter anchor. The mezcal here keeps it honest.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More bitter, less sweet orange — pushes toward a mezcal Negroni riff. Worth exploring.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Softer and more honey-forward than green. The correct choice — green overwhelms the balance.

steps: Combine all four ingredients in a shaker with ice.
Shake vigorously for 10–12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
No garnish needed.
notes: Equal parts discipline: This drink only works in balance. Don't eyeball — measure all four ingredients.
Yellow vs Green Chartreuse: Yellow only. Green makes a harder, less integrated drink here.
Variation — Naked and Smoked: Replace ¼ oz of the mezcal with Laphroaig. The peat pushes the drink firmly into your wheelhouse.
history: Created by Joaquín Simó at Death & Co in New York, the Naked and Famous is a direct riff on the Paper Plane. It replaced bourbon with mezcal and Amaro Nonino with Aperol, creating a version that's simultaneously more approachable and more interesting.

name: De La Louisiane
desc: A Vieux Carré cousin — rye, Bénédictine, sweet vermouth, Peychaud's, with an absinthe rinse. The anise thread from Peychaud's and the rinse weaves through every sip without announcing itself.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: High proof is essential — both the absinthe rinse and Peychaud's want a bold rye to stand against.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: The New Orleans native choice — the absinthe rinse reads as more prominent, authentic to the Sazerac tradition.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Rich and chocolatey — good foundation for the Bénédictine.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: The richer choice — Bénédictine plays off Carpano's complexity beautifully.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The anise and floral qualities connect the absinthe rinse to the body of the drink. No substitutes.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Clean, traditional, anise-forward. A small pour to coat the glass.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Higher quality with more botanical complexity.

steps: Rinse the coupe: add a small pour of absinthe (about ¼ tsp), swirl to coat the glass, and discard the excess.
Combine rye, sweet vermouth, Bénédictine, and Peychaud's in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds until well-chilled.
Strain into the absinthe-rinsed coupe.
Garnish with a Luxardo cherry.
notes: The absinthe rinse is a technique: You get the anise aroma and a ghost of flavor without absinthe dominating. Don't add it directly to the build.
Peychaud's is specific: The anise connects the rinse to the body of the drink. Angostura doesn't carry that note.
Variation — Improved Whiskey Cocktail: The ancestor of this style — rye, maraschino instead of Bénédictine, absinthe rinse, bitters. Drier and more austere.
history: The De La Louisiane dates to at least 1937, named for the Restaurant de la Louisiane in New Orleans. Like the Vieux Carré, it's built on the intersection of American rye, European liqueurs, and the New Orleans tradition of absinthe as aromatic seasoning.

name: Scotch Boulevardier
desc: A Negroni with bourbon replaced by blended Scotch. The drink gets smokier, drier, and more complex — same structural logic, different soul entirely.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Light smoke, malty backbone. Lets Campari and vermouth participate as equal partners.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Richer and slightly sweeter. Campari reads as more assertive as a result.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Heavily peated blended malt. Smoke becomes the dominant character — closer to your palate.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Rich and chocolatey — holds up beautifully against Campari.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: The classic Negroni/Boulevardier pairing.

steps: Combine Scotch, Campari, and sweet vermouth in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds.
Strain over a large single ice cube.
Express orange peel, run around the rim, and drop in.
notes: Ratio flexibility: This build uses 1½ oz Scotch for a more spirit-forward drink. The classic ratio is 1:1:1 — try both.
Campari is genuinely bitter: Scotch provides smoke and malt, Campari provides intense orange bitterness, vermouth provides just enough sweetness to hold the structure.
Variation — Smoked Negroni: Replace half the Scotch with mezcal (¾ oz each). Smoke comes from two directions — peat and agave.
history: The Boulevardier was created by American expat Erskine Gwynne in Paris and published in 1927. The Scotch substitution evolved naturally as bartenders explored the Negroni template with different spirits.

name: Smoked Reposado Margarita
desc: A dry, spirit-forward margarita on a tequila-mezcal split. No sweet mix, no sugar rim — clean agave, citrus, and smoke in proper proportion.
glass: Rocks glass · Ice · Half salt rim

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Women-owned Jalisco distillery, clean and slightly oaky.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More earthy and agave-forward.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: One of the most respected small-production reposados.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Artesanal production, 100% agave — solid and smoky without aggression.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: The benchmark. Earthy, fruity, subtly smoky — integrates seamlessly.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Push mezcal to 1 oz and drop tequila to 1 oz. Smoke becomes the primary character.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Cognac-based, drier and more complex than generic triple sec.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Darker and more brandy-forward. The drink becomes richer and slightly heavier.

steps: Half-rim the glass: run a lime wedge around one side only, press into kosher salt on a plate. Fill the glass with ice.
Combine tequila, mezcal, fresh lime juice, Cointreau, agave syrup, and a pinch of kosher salt in the shaker with ice.
Shake vigorously for 10–12 seconds.
Strain into the prepared rocks glass over fresh ice.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
notes: Half-rim the salt: Salting the full rim forces every sip through salt. The half-rim lets you choose your ratio sip by sip.
Mezcal ratio: ½ oz keeps smoke as a presence. Push to ¾ oz to make it a co-star. Equal parts (1:1) is a full mezcal margarita — a different and valid drink.
The agave syrup: ¼ oz is structural. More than this and you've crossed into sweet mix territory.
Variation — Tommy's Margarita: Drop the Cointreau entirely, use ½ oz agave syrup instead. The spirit-forward purist's version.
history: The margarita's origins are genuinely contested — at least a dozen bartenders claimed credit between the 1930s and 1950s. The mezcal margarita is a product of the craft cocktail revival, as bartenders recognized mezcal's smoke brought something to the template that blanco tequila didn't.

name: The Winnequah
desc: A custom original built on a rye–Islay Scotch split. Smoke and spice as co-equals, bridged by Bénédictine, deepened by Barolo Chinato, with Peychaud's and a whisper of absinthe weaving anise through without announcing it. Built specifically for your palate.
glass: Coupe or Nick & Nora · Large rock

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Big, spicy, assertive — holds its own against Laphroaig as a true co-equal.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Madeira, Sauternes, and Cognac cask finishes create a wine-and-dried-fruit layer that amplifies the Barolo Chinato specifically.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Phenolic, iodine, seaweed smoke — what this drink was built around.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Campfire and charcoal rather than Laphroaig's medicinal iodine. Slightly more elegant.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Deep, complex, dried fruit and massive smoke. The Winnequah becomes a slower, more contemplative drink.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The essential ingredient — bitter wine, quinine, spice. No substitute exists.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The anise quality connects to the absinthe drop and creates the drink's through-line.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: One drop in the build — not a rinse. Fully integrated anise whisper woven through every sip.

steps: Add one drop of absinthe directly to the mixing glass before ice — it integrates into the base rather than sitting as a surface note.
Add rye, Laphroaig, Barolo Chinato, Bénédictine, and Peychaud's bitters. Fill with ice.
Stir for 25–30 seconds — slightly longer than usual to let the Laphroaig fully integrate.
Strain over a large rock in a coupe or Nick & Nora.
Express a lemon peel over the glass to release the citrus oils, then discard. Do not drop it in.
notes: Express and discard: The lemon oils lift the smoke and spice aromatics — but the peel's continued presence in the glass is not wanted.
Absinthe in the build: One drop integrates fully. A rinse puts anise on the surface; in the build it's woven through every sip.
Barolo Chinato is irreplaceable: Sweet vermouth doesn't work here. This drink was designed around that specific bottle.
Variation — The Winnequah Lighter: Reduce Laphroaig to ½ oz and add ½ oz additional rye. More accessible, less smoke-dominant.
history: An original creation built from your palate profile — the through-lines of smoke (Laphroaig), anise (Peychaud's, absinthe), herbal depth (Bénédictine), and bitter wine complexity (Barolo Chinato) that emerged from an evening at The Aviary in Chicago. Named for a place that carries personal meaning. There is no other copy of this drink.

name: The Black Irish
desc: An Irish whiskey Old Fashioned built around coffee liqueur and mole bitters. Single pot still Irish is your wheelhouse's near neighbor — lighter than rye but the bitter coffee modifier and mole bitters push it into familiar complex territory.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The defining single pot still expression. Rich, oily, and complex with dried fruit and spice. This is the bottle that converts rye drinkers.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More grain-forward and lighter than Redbreast. Lets the coffee liqueur become more prominent.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: More Sherry cask influence — dried fruit and walnut notes that amplify the coffee modifier beautifully.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.bottle: Mr Black Cold Brew Coffee Liqueur
tiers.note: Lower sugar than Kahlúa, genuinely coffee-forward. The right choice.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Italian espresso-based, drier and more intense. The drink becomes more austere — closer to your palate profile.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The chocolate-chili combination bridges coffee and Irish whiskey in a way no other bitters do.

steps: Combine Irish whiskey, coffee liqueur, demerara syrup, and bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds.
Strain over a large ice cube.
Express orange peel and drop it in.
notes: Why single pot still Irish: Blended Irish is light and simple. Single pot still — Redbreast, Green Spot — is oily, rich, and spice-forward. More in common with rye than its reputation suggests.
Coffee as modifier: This is not a dessert drink. ½ oz coffee liqueur works like Averna in a Black Manhattan — adding bitter complexity, not flavoring.
Variation — Espresso Old Fashioned: Replace the coffee liqueur with 1 oz cold brew concentrate and ¼ oz simple syrup. More bitter, less sweet.
history: This build ignores the unfortunately sweet Irish coffee cocktail lineage entirely and treats single pot still Irish the way a Manhattan treats rye. The category was nearly extinct by the 1990s but was revived by Redbreast and a handful of distilleries who recognized it as one of the world's truly distinctive whiskey styles.

name: White Negroni
desc: A gin Negroni variant that replaces Campari with Suze (French gentian bitter) and sweet vermouth with Lillet Blanc. The Suze's gentian root bitterness is intensely herbal and assertive — more complex and less sweet than Campari.
glass: Chilled coupe or rocks with large ice

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Juniper-forward and dry. High proof, holds its own against Suze's intensity.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Cucumber and rose alongside juniper. The floral quality softens the Suze — a more approachable version.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Made at Bruichladdich on Islay — 22 foraged island botanicals. Maritime character creates an unexpected connection to your Scotch preferences.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: French, gentian root-based, intensely bitter and earthy with floral notes. Not Campari — the bitterness is more herbal. Try it on ice alone first.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: French wine-based aperitif — lighter and more floral than sweet vermouth.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More bitter and quinine-forward than Lillet. The whole drink gets more austere — significantly closer to your palate profile.

steps: Combine gin, Suze, and Lillet Blanc (or Cocchi Americano) in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe, or over a large rock.
Express lemon peel and drop in or discard.
notes: Why gin might work for you: London Dry gin is not sweet — a gin Negroni variant built around Suze's gentian bitterness is about as far from a fruity gin drink as possible.
Try Suze first: Before making this drink, try a small pour of Suze on ice. The gentian root bitterness is the missing link between your amaro preferences and the gin world.
The Botanist connection: Made at Bruichladdich on Islay. It doesn't taste like Scotch, but the maritime botanicals create a thread that makes the gin feel less foreign.
history: Created by Wayne Collins in France around 2001 when he couldn't find Campari and substituted Suze and Lillet Blanc. It's now considered one of the most important Negroni variations because it demonstrated that the Campari/sweet vermouth/gin structure is a template, not a formula.

name: The Dirty Martini (Done Right)
desc: The vodka cocktail your palate can actually get behind — not because vodka is interesting, but because olive brine and dry vermouth are. When built properly, salinity and bitterness carry the drink.
glass: Chilled coupe · No ice · Very cold

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Clean, slightly creamy, neutral. The correct cocktail vodka — not flavorless but not distracting.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Polish rye vodka — subtle grain character gives more presence.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: French wheat vodka, extraordinarily smooth. The brine and vermouth carry even more of the weight.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Clean and crisp. Don't skip this — a Martini without vermouth is cold vodka, not a cocktail.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More oxidized and complex — hints of almond and herbs. The drink becomes noticeably more interesting.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Buttery, mild, slightly sweet brine from Sicilian green olives. The dirty martini made with this is a fundamentally better drink than the bar standard.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Made specifically for cocktails — filtered, balanced, and consistent.

steps: Chill your coupe in the freezer for at least 5 minutes — temperature is critical in a Martini.
Combine vodka, dry vermouth, and olive brine in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 30 seconds — longer than most cocktails. Dilution and temperature are everything here.
Strain into the chilled coupe.
Garnish with 2–3 Castelvetrano olives on a pick.
notes: Why this might work: The dirty martini is primarily a salt-and-bitter drink when made with quality brine and real vermouth. It hits the same notes you like in stirred spirit-forward cocktails — salinity as the bitter counterbalance instead of amaro.
Temperature is everything: The glass must be cold, the stir must be long, and it should be consumed before it warms.
Castelvetrano specifically: Buttery, meaty olives produce more complex brine. The eating experience at the bottom of the glass is part of the drink.
Going deeper — 50/50 Martini: Equal parts vodka and dry vermouth (1½ oz each), less brine. More aromatic, lower ABV. The drink your great-grandfather actually drank.
history: The Martini is the most argued-over cocktail in history. The dirty Martini dates to at least 1901, credited to New York bartender John O'Connor. The key upgrade that changes everything: quality brine from quality olives. The rest of the arguments are mostly noise.

name: Greenpoint
desc: A Manhattan riff from the Brooklyn cocktail family. Rye and sweet vermouth as the base, with yellow Chartreuse stepping in where Bénédictine sits in the Vieux Carré — adding herbal, honeyed complexity without taking over. Both bitters, lemon twist.
glass: Chilled coupe · or rocks over large cube

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The spice and proof are essential here — the Chartreuse is assertive and a low-proof rye gets absorbed rather than balanced.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More rounded and honeyed, which echoes the Chartreuse's honey notes rather than contrasting them. A richer, more integrated drink.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: More floral and complex than younger ryes. The Chartreuse becomes a complement rather than a modifier — the two herbaceous elements weave together.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Honey, saffron, and 130 alpine herbs. Softer and sweeter than green — the correct choice here. Green Chartreuse is too aggressive and high-proof for this balance.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Rich and chocolatey — holds its own alongside the Chartreuse without competing with it.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More bitter than standard sweet vermouth — adds a bitter-orange backbone that tightens the whole drink. Several bartenders consider this the better choice for the Greenpoint specifically. Changes the character toward more assertive bitterness.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The dry, spicy orange note lifts the Chartreuse's herbal character. Both bitters are needed — Angostura alone makes this too heavy.

steps: Chill your coupe or rocks glass while you build the drink.
Combine rye, Chartreuse, sweet vermouth, and both bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds until well-chilled.
Strain into your chilled glass — coupe up, or over a large single cube on the rocks.
Express lemon twist over the surface to release the oils, then drop it in.
notes: Lemon over orange: The original calls for lemon twist, and it's correct — the Chartreuse's herbal and honey notes are lifted by citrus in a way orange doesn't quite achieve. Don't swap it.

Punt e Mes variation: Worth trying on the second round. Punt e Mes is a bitter-sweet vermouth (Campari and vermouth in one bottle, essentially) — it shifts the Greenpoint toward more bitter, less sweet. Closer to your usual preference.

Why this fits your wheelhouse: The structure is pure Manhattan family. The Chartreuse is doing the same job Bénédictine does in the Vieux Carré — herbal complexity woven through a rye-and-vermouth base. If you love the Vieux Carré, this should land similarly.

Variation — Smoky Greenpoint: Swap the rye for a peated blended Scotch. The Chartreuse reads completely differently against smoke — more alpine forest than honey-herb. An interesting direction worth exploring.
history: Created by Michael McIlroy at Milk & Honey in New York City in 2006, the Greenpoint is part of an unofficial series of Brooklyn neighborhood cocktails — alongside the Red Hook, the Slope, and the Carroll Gardens — each a Manhattan riff with a different modifier. McIlroy named it for the northernmost neighborhood of Brooklyn, known at the time as a gritty, overlooked corner of the city that was quietly excellent. The drink has the same character: understated, complex, better than it looks on paper.

name: Mezcal Negroni
desc: The Negroni template with mezcal replacing gin. Equal parts mezcal, Campari, sweet vermouth. The smoke reframes Campari's bitterness entirely — less candy-orange, more charred and complex. Built entirely from bottles you already own.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The benchmark — earthy, fruity, subtle smoke. Integrates with Campari without dominating it. The classic choice for this build.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Smokier and more mineral than Vida. The Campari's bitterness becomes a counterbalance to the smoke rather than a co-equal. Pushes the drink closer to your palate profile.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.bottle: Del Maguey San Luis del Rio
tiers.note: Single-village, complex and intensely smoky. The Campari is almost a seasoning at this point — mezcal is fully in charge. A very different and more challenging drink.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Rich and chocolatey — the chocolate note plays beautifully against mezcal's smoke.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More vanilla and dried fruit. The drink becomes richer and slightly heavier — a more opulent version of the same structure.

steps: Combine mezcal, Campari, and sweet vermouth in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds.
Strain over a large single ice cube in a rocks glass.
Express orange peel over the glass, run it around the rim, and drop it in.
notes: Why mezcal over gin: Gin brings botanical complexity that can fight with Campari. Mezcal brings smoke that reframes Campari's bitterness — the orange-bitter note becomes earthier and more complex rather than candy-forward.
Equal parts is the discipline: The Negroni template only works in balance. Don't adjust ratios until you've made it at spec and know which direction you want to push.

Variation — bump the mezcal: Go 1½ oz mezcal, ¾ oz Campari, ¾ oz vermouth for a more spirit-forward, less bitter version. This is how the Scotch Boulevardier is built — more base spirit, less modifier.
Variation — Oaxacan Negroni: Use ½ oz mezcal and ½ oz reposado tequila as the base. The agave complexity doubles — smoke plus oak — and Campari has more to work against.
history: The Mezcal Negroni has no single credited inventor — it emerged naturally as mezcal became a serious cocktail spirit in the early 2010s and bartenders began substituting it into classic templates. The Negroni itself dates to 1919, when Count Camillo Negroni asked a Florence bartender to strengthen his Americano by replacing the soda water with gin. The mezcal substitution took a century to arrive but has become one of the most popular modern riffs — it turns out that smoke and Campari's bitterness are a better match than gin's botanicals and Campari's bitterness.

name: Frisco Sour
desc: Three ingredients: rye, Bénédictine, fresh lemon. Bénédictine does the work of both modifier and sweetener simultaneously. The result is herbal, honeyed, and surprisingly complex for how simple the build is — the closest thing to a pure Bénédictine showcase in cocktail form.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The spice and proof are essential — Bénédictine is sweet and herbal, and a big rye prevents this from reading as dessert.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More floral and delicate than Rittenhouse. The Bénédictine becomes more prominent — a slightly more Bénédictine-forward expression of the same drink.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: 27 plants and spices — angelica, hyssop, saffron, honey, and a dozen other things the monks have kept secret since 1510. This is the drink that makes you understand what Bénédictine actually is.

steps: Combine rye, Bénédictine, and fresh lemon juice in a shaker with ice.
Shake vigorously for 10–12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist or Luxardo cherry.
notes: Why it's in Further Afield: The sour format is outside your usual preference — but this one earns its place because the lemon is doing structural work, not flavoring work. The Bénédictine's sweetness and herbal complexity are big enough that the lemon just provides the tension to make them readable.

Bénédictine as the star: You've been using Bénédictine as a supporting modifier in the Vieux Carré, De La Louisiane, and The Winnequah. This is the drink where you find out what it tastes like when it's in charge. Worth making once for that reason alone.
Fresh lemon only: Three ingredients means nowhere to hide. Bottled lemon juice kills this drink.

Variation — B&B Sour: Replace half the Bénédictine with brandy (¼ oz Bénédictine, ¼ oz cognac, keep the rest). B&B is a classic pre-made blend of the two — this essentially recreates it in sour format. Slightly less sweet, more complex.
history: The Frisco Sour dates to at least the 1930s, named for San Francisco and built on the simplest possible premise: Bénédictine is sweet and herbal, rye is spicy and spirit-forward, lemon cuts both. It predates the craft cocktail era by decades and was largely forgotten until bartenders rediscovered it as a showcase for Bénédictine specifically. The D.O.M. on the bottle stands for Deo Optimo Maximo — To God, Most Good, Most Great — which the Benedictine monks of Fécamp have been putting on the label since 1510, when a monk named Dom Bernardo Vincelli allegedly created the original formula.

name: Espresso Martini
desc: The crowd-pleaser that actually deserves its reputation when made properly — cold espresso, vodka, quality coffee liqueur, shaken hard for that signature foam. The Friends version; see notes for a spirit-forward variation built around your palate.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Clean and neutral — lets the espresso lead. The correct base for the standard build.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.bottle: Fresh espresso or cold brew concentrate
tiers.note: Fresh espresso shaken cold produces the best foam. Cold brew concentrate works but produces less crema. Instant espresso powder dissolved in hot water is an acceptable backup.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.bottle: Mr Black Cold Brew Coffee Liqueur
tiers.note: Lower sugar than Kahlúa, genuinely coffee-forward. The drink tastes like coffee, not coffee candy.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Drier and more intense than Mr Black. The drink becomes more austere and less sweet — the version guests who like serious cocktails will prefer.

steps: Pull espresso and let it cool slightly — or use cold brew concentrate. Hot espresso will melt the ice too fast and dilute the drink.
Combine vodka, espresso, coffee liqueur, and simple syrup in a shaker with ice.
Shake very hard for 12–15 seconds — harder and longer than most cocktails. The vigorous shake is what creates the foam.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe. The foam should settle on top within a few seconds.
Garnish with three coffee beans arranged in the center of the foam.
notes: The foam: It comes from the espresso's crema being agitated by shaking. If there's no foam, the espresso was too old, too cool, or the shake wasn't hard enough. Fresh espresso = better foam, every time.
Three coffee beans: Traditional garnish representing health, wealth, and happiness. Also functional — the scent hits before the first sip.

For your palate — The Rye Espresso Martini: Replace the vodka with 1 oz rye (Rittenhouse) and ½ oz vodka. Swap the coffee liqueur for Borghetti. Drop the simple syrup entirely — the rye's sweetness does that job. The result is a spirit-forward, bitter, coffee-driven drink that fits your wheelhouse while still being recognizable to guests as an espresso martini.
Further variation: Add a single dash of Angostura to the rye version. The bitters bridge the coffee and whiskey exactly the way they do in the Black Irish.
history: The Espresso Martini was created by Dick Bradsell at the Soho Brasserie in London in 1983. The story — probably true — is that a young model asked him for a drink that would 'wake me up and then f*** me up.' Bradsell reached for the espresso machine next to his bar and built what was then called a Vodka Espresso. It was renamed the Espresso Martini in the 1990s and became one of the defining drinks of that decade, fell out of fashion, and was dramatically revived during the 2020s to become arguably the most ordered cocktail in the world. The revival is largely deserved — when made with quality espresso and coffee liqueur, it's a genuinely good drink.

name: Gold Rush
desc: A three-ingredient bourbon sour built on honey syrup instead of simple. The honey rounds the bourbon's edges in a way sugar doesn't. Crowd-pleasing, easy to make in batches, and genuinely delicious. See notes for a more complex version that fits your palate.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Approachable, well-priced, crowd-friendly. The right call when making these for guests — you don't need a premium bourbon in a sour.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More complexity and proof than Buffalo Trace without becoming intimidating. Guests who notice bourbon will notice this.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Rich, spice-forward, and well-known by name — guests who like to see a recognizable bottle will appreciate this.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: 3 parts honey to 1 part warm water. Stir until dissolved, cool, refrigerate up to 2 weeks. The 3:1 ratio keeps it honey-forward without being too thick.

steps: Make honey syrup ahead: combine 3 parts honey and 1 part warm water, stir until fully dissolved, cool, refrigerate.
Combine bourbon, honey syrup, and fresh lemon juice in a shaker with ice.
Shake vigorously for 10–12 seconds.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
No garnish needed, though a lemon wheel or expressed peel is a nice touch.
notes: Batch-friendly: This is one of the easiest cocktails to pre-batch for a group. Combine bourbon and honey syrup ahead of time (juice separately — don't pre-mix citrus). Add fresh lemon when shaking to order, or shake the full batch with ice and strain into a pitcher.
3:1 honey syrup: The ratio matters. 1:1 honey syrup is too thin and sweet; straight honey is too thick to integrate. 3:1 (honey:water) pours cleanly and keeps the flavor concentrated.

For your palate — The Gold Rush with depth: Keep the base recipe, but add ¼ oz Bénédictine and two dashes of Angostura. The Bénédictine echoes the honey's sweetness while adding herbal complexity; the Angostura provides the bitters structure you prefer. Barely different to make, dramatically more interesting to drink.
Further variation: Replace the bourbon with rye for a sharper, more spirit-forward version. The honey becomes a counterbalance rather than a complement — a more demanding drink.
history: Created by T.J. Siegel at Milk & Honey in New York City around 2000, the Gold Rush is one of the most important cocktails of the modern craft era. Its significance is less about the recipe — which is beautifully simple — and more about what it demonstrated: that honey syrup makes a fundamentally better sour than simple syrup, and that a three-ingredient cocktail can be more interesting than a five-ingredient one. It sparked a wave of honey-based cocktails and remains the definitive example of ingredient substitution changing a drink's entire character.

name: Gin & Tonic
desc: The most ordered cocktail in the world for good reason — when made with quality gin and quality tonic, it's simple, refreshing, and endlessly variable. The Friends version is classic; the notes contain a mezcal-tonic variation built specifically for your palate.
glass: Highball or large wine glass · plenty of ice

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Juniper-forward and dry. The classic G&T gin — its assertiveness holds up against tonic better than more delicate gins.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Cucumber and rose — pairs particularly well with a cucumber garnish and a more floral tonic. Good for guests who find straight gin too aggressive.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: 22 foraged Islay botanicals. Maritime, herbal, complex. The G&T becomes a serious drink — guests who appreciate whisky complexity will respond to this.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The gold standard for premium tonic. Real quinine, balanced bitterness, not overly sweet. The difference between Fever-Tree and grocery store tonic is significant.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More bitter and herbal than Indian Tonic — adds complexity that pairs well with assertive gins. The variation to use for your palate.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: More bitter and less sweet than Fever-Tree — the most sophisticated mainstream tonic available. Expensive but worth having for serious gin.

steps: Fill a highball glass or large wine glass completely with ice — more ice than you think you need. More ice means slower dilution and a colder drink.
Pour gin over the ice.
Pour tonic slowly down the side of the glass to preserve carbonation — don't pour over the ice directly.
Stir gently once or twice with a bar spoon — just enough to combine.
Squeeze a lime wedge over the top and drop it in.
notes: Ice matters more than you think: A G&T with insufficient ice dilutes quickly and gets warm. Fill the glass completely — it's not being cheap with the drink, it's keeping it cold longer.
Pour the tonic slowly: Pouring directly over ice destroys carbonation. Down the side of the glass preserves the bubbles, which are half the drink.

For your palate — The Mezcal Tonic: Replace the gin with 1½ oz Del Maguey Vida mezcal. Use Fever-Tree Aromatic Tonic (more bitter, more herbal). Add 2 dashes orange bitters and garnish with a lime wheel and a pinch of salt on the rim. The smoke from the mezcal plays against the tonic's quinine bitterness in a way that's surprisingly compelling — more interesting than a standard G&T and entirely your wheelhouse.
Batch tip: Pre-measure and combine gin portions ahead of time. Add tonic and ice to order — never pre-mix the tonic, as it will go flat immediately.
Garnish variation: Cucumber and fresh mint work beautifully with Hendrick's specifically. Orange peel with Tanqueray. The garnish should complement the gin's botanical profile.
history: The Gin & Tonic was born from the British Empire's need to get quinine into its soldiers in India to prevent malaria. Quinine — the active ingredient in tonic water — is intensely bitter on its own, so officers began mixing it with gin, sugar, and lime to make it palatable. The 'Indian tonic water' name is a direct reference to this origin. By the mid-1800s it was a colonial staple; by the 20th century it was a global default; by the 21st century the craft tonic movement — led by Fever-Tree's founding in 2004 — transformed it from a basic drink into a serious one. The Spanish gin-tonic movement, which uses large wine glasses, premium gin, craft tonic, and botanical garnishes, did the most to elevate the format to its current status.
